nameStory: The Louisiana Painted-Dark bee gets its curious name from being first scientifically described from Louisiana specimens, though it ranges much wider across eastern North America. The 'painted-dark' part refers to its distinctive dark coloration with subtle lighter markings that look like delicate brushstrokes against its dusky body.
description: The Louisiana Painted-Dark bee is a small, dark-colored cuckoo bee that belongs to the mason and leafcutter bee family. Like other cuckoo bees, it doesn't build its own nest or collect pollen - instead, it sneaks into other bees' nests to lay its eggs, letting the host bee raise its young. These compact bees have a sleek, somewhat shiny appearance with dark bodies marked by lighter patches or bands. They're active fliers that you might spot visiting sunflowers and other blooms from spring through fall.

idTips.label: Dark, sleek body
idTips.description: Overall dark brown to black coloration with a smooth, somewhat shiny surface that catches light differently than fuzzy bees

idTips.label: Compact build
idTips.description: Small, streamlined body shape without the heavy fuzziness of pollen-collecting bees - feels smooth if handled gently

idTips.label: Light markings
idTips.description: Subtle pale or whitish bands or spots on the abdomen that contrast with the dark background

idTips.label: Quick flight pattern
idTips.description: Fast, darting flight style as they search for host nests or nectar sources, less methodical than pollen collectors

idTips.label: Sunflower visitor
idTips.description: Often seen on large composite flowers like sunflowers, where their dark bodies stand out against yellow petals

habitat: Look for Louisiana Painted-Dark bees in areas where their host bees nest, typically sunny open spaces with sandy or well-drained soil where mason and leafcutter bees are active. They frequent gardens, meadows, and woodland edges where flowering plants provide nectar sources. You'll often spot them near sunflower patches, native wildflower areas, and anywhere their host bees are building nests in hollow stems or soil cavities.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in March and become active as temperatures warm, searching for early host nests and spring flowers for nectar.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're most commonly seen visiting flowers and parasitizing host bee nests throughout the warm months.
seasonality.fall: Activity continues into September as late-season flowers provide nectar, with the last individuals completing their reproductive cycle.
seasonality.winter: Overwintering as developing larvae in host bee nests, completely inactive and hidden from view.

funFact: This bee is essentially a 'con artist' of the insect world - the female sneaks into another bee's carefully provisioned nest, lays her egg, and her larva will actually eat both the host's egg and all the pollen and nectar the hardworking mother bee collected for her own offspring!
confusionNotes: Can be confused with other small dark bees, but most native bees you'll see are fuzzy pollen collectors, while this cuckoo bee has a sleek, less hairy appearance. Remember: if it looks too smooth and shiny to be carrying pollen effectively, it might be a cuckoo bee like this one.
contextualKnowledge: The name 'cuckoo bee' comes from the same parasitic behavior as cuckoo birds - laying eggs in another species' nest and letting them do all the work of raising the young. Despite this seemingly harsh lifestyle, cuckoo bees are a natural part of the ecosystem and don't significantly harm their host bee populations.
compareHints: Louisiana Painted-Dark bees are distinguished from other dark bees in their genus by their specific distribution in eastern North America and their tendency to visit sunflowers. Compared to the Compressed Dark Bee, they have a less constricted waist, and unlike the Spot-sided Dark Bee, their light markings are more band-like than distinctly spotted on the sides.
